column3: Directly restates the prohibition on exaltation and frames it as resistance to divine authority.
Pairs denial of the one God with active arrogance, clarifying the focus's rejected posture.
Names submission as a conscious response of belief, though outside the political confrontation.
Defines believers as those who remain submitting, reinforcing the destination named in the focus.
Begins the letter-delivery sequence whose reply is stated in the focus.
Shows surrender when false claims collapse, contrasting the focus's demanded voluntary submission.
Continues the same encounter and explicitly anticipates their coming as submitters.
Establishes the queen's endowed rule and throne, the authority challenged by the letter.
Joins God's oneness to the direct question of whether hearers will submit.
Uses coming to a ruler in a distant family-reconciliation setting only.
Opposes serving a rebellious power, a secondary contrast to abandoning exalted autonomy.
Its rejected elevation reading is only a boundary contrast, not support for the focus.
The delayed wish to be submitters sharpens the cost of refusing submission now.
Records the queen receiving the noble letter immediately before its quoted demand.

The Pharaoh context supplies a limited parallel to confronting a ruling people.

Satan's embellishment of deeds supplies only a broad backdrop for resistant communities.
Submission is defined by refusing rival loyalties, relevant to the focus's exclusive authority.
A prayer to die as submitters is a distant endurance parallel.
Identifies Solomon and invokes God at the opening of the letter continued by the focus.
Presents submission as faithful resolve under threat rather than capitulation.

Names the sun-worship and misguidance underlying the focus's summons away from false allegiance.
The rejected peace-formula reading adds no usable relation to the command.
Rejects making people lords and ends with a declaration of submission, closely matching the focus's logic.
The ownership analogy only distantly touches unequal authority.
Eschatological entry in peace does not clarify the focus's political-religious summons.
A direct monotheistic prohibition supports the demand to abandon competing allegiance.
Shows the queen consulting her council as the immediate response to the letter.
Describes Pharaoh as arrogantly elevated, a close model of the posture rejected in the focus.
God's transcendent height gives only a broad contrast to human overreaching.
Later in the surah, submission marks those able to receive guidance, extending the response theme.
The greeting of peace has no material link to the demanded submission.
Divine control of favor does not add to the focus's confrontation with rule.
Links Islam with receptive openness, a secondary illumination of coming in submission.

Disobedience to a command is too general after stronger command parallels.

Commands submission to the one God, though without the focus's conflict over authority.
The punishment scene offers no distinct connection to the focus.
Universal coming humbled on the Last Day is a remote counterpart to coming as submitters.
The queen's final confession and submission provide the narrative resolution of the focus.
Noah's exclusive-worship summons parallels the religious demand within the letter.
Mercy toward sinners does not clarify self-exaltation or the requested response.
Compelled surrender after collapse contrasts with the focus's demanded submission before coercion.
A trading condition requiring arrival is only a lexical echo.
The queen describes kings humiliating a town's honored people, clarifying the stakes of political domination.
The command to submit receives an immediate affirmative answer, echoing the focus's imperative.
The inability to speak or excuse oneself does not add to the focus.

Forced surrender paired with denial of wrongdoing contrasts with sincere submission.
Makes trust in God the consequence of being submitters in a Pharaoh confrontation.
Avoiding idols supports exclusive loyalty but is less specific than earlier monotheism cards.
In the same surah, knowing rejection is attributed to injustice and self-exaltation.
Moses' demand to yield God's servants forms the immediate prophetic setting for 44:19's ban on exaltation.
The queen's proposed gift advances the same negotiation after the focus's letter.
The peace formula adds no distinct connection after other submission material.
The failure to accord God due gravity offers a broad inverse of abandoning proud rule.
Its local monotheistic challenge is secondary to the letter's direct demand.
Combines calling to God with openly naming oneself among the submitters.
The request to bring materials has no material relation to the focus.
Destroyed stronger towns give only a distant warning against political confidence.
Defines submission to God through a directed, beneficent life rather than a label alone.
Persistent disbelief does not add a distinct facet to the demand.
Solomon rejects the gift, the next decisive response within the same confrontation.
Being commanded to be first among submitters reinforces submission as enacted obedience.
The offer in Lot's narrative has no useful relation to the focus.
The nearby declaration about those who cannot hear gives only a general limit on persuasion.
God's supreme height is a general corrective to human claims of height.
The prayer for a submitting community is a broad communal parallel.
Exclusive knowledge of God offers only a general monotheistic backdrop.
The injunction to die submitting is a remote continuity-of-faith parallel.
The prohibition on transgression gives a limited boundary against overreach.
The threatened return and arrival in humiliation is the letter's direct escalation after the focus.
Contrasts submitters with criminals, resisting any equation of submission with unaccountable privilege.
Those who recognize the revelation declare prior submission, a substantive recognition parallel.
The local monotheistic question remains a general support for exclusive divine authority.
Separates God's true transcendence from the human domination implied by arrogant elevation.
The blessing on Moses and Aaron is only a lexical peace echo.
A declaration of faith before a people offers a distant summons-and-response parallel.
A family confession of worship and submission is less specific than earlier formulations.
Joseph's prayer to die submitting connects entrusted rule with continued dependence on God.

Links corruption with great self-exaltation, offering a historical counterpart to the focus's prohibition.

The provision-of-water verse has no useful connection to the focus.

The plain-warning role is a limited prophetic-summons parallel.

Physical elevation of a prophet does not illuminate arrogant elevation.
The messenger's teaching and purification give a broad setting for receiving revelation.
Marking the nose has no useful relation to submission or authority.
Noah's sustained calling offers a distant parallel to delivering a summons.
The exception for the people of the right has no distinct connection.
The distinction between believers is not tied to the focus's demand.
Moses receiving the Book gives only a broad precedent for authoritative divine communication.
Humble prayer and answered devotion form a remote contrast to self-exaltation.
Completes the account of the queen's people by identifying their withheld prostration to God.
Names God alone as deity and Lord of the great throne, directly recasting the contest over royal authority.
The jinn's offer to bring the throne opens the power demonstration that prepares the queen's recognition.
The throne's swift arrival explicitly tests gratitude and makes royal power answerable to God.
The altered throne tests whether recognition can become guidance before the queen's submission.
States that prior worship barred the queen, supplying the obstacle overcome by her final confession.
Commands the messenger to declare submission to God and confronts hearers with the same decision.
Sets willing and unwilling universal submission before God against autonomous claims of rule.
Treats Islam as the accepted orientation, reinforcing the consequence of the focus's summons.
Defines the best religious orientation as submitting one's face to God while doing good.
Rejects turning to powerless rivals and commands submission to the Lord of all worlds.
Dedicates worship and life to God alone, a concrete form of the exclusive allegiance sought in the focus.
Condemns those who act arrogantly on earth without right and are turned from the signs.
Pharaoh's belated claim to be among submitters provides a stark contrast to timely submission.
Explicitly states that God does not love the arrogant, directly judging the focus's forbidden posture.
Forbids walking exultantly on earth, a practical boundary against self-exaltation.
Describes Pharaoh and his chiefs as arrogant and elevated, closely paralleling the rejected conduct.
Pharaoh's self-exaltation in the land shows its political consequence in dividing and oppressing people.
Links arrogant self-exaltation to denial of return to God, extending the focus's authority critique.
Combines the confession of one God with the declaration that believers are submitters to Him.
Defines secure devotion as submitting one's face to God while doing good.
Calls people to turn and submit to their Lord before coercive punishment makes the choice too late.
Associates arrogance and domination with a sealed heart, explaining resistance to divine authority.
Identifies disputants who act arrogantly without warrant, a close pattern of illegitimate elevation.
